item.title: Netflix’s the New Stanford Prison Experiment
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Netflix’s the New Stanford Prison Experiment

Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment continues to resonate with the public

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • The Stanford Prison Experiment (SPE) remains one of the most infamous studies in the field.
  • Contemporary research has questioned the scientific legitimacy of the research design of the SPE.
  • The SPE continues to capture the imagination of the public.
  • Does a reality television reimagining of The SPE have anything meaningful to contribute?

I imagine my skeptical and slightly horrified reaction when I heard about Netflix’s attempt to replicate Philip Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment from the 1970s was similar to that of many other social psychologists and academics. In fact, a fellow grad student—and dear friend—from my doctorate program was the one who alerted me to the release of this new show, and we exchanged a series of predictable messages bemoaning the lack of scientific viability behind such an attempt.

The Stanford Prison Experiment was part of a number of studies spanning the 1950s-70s in the field of social psychology that shed light on the situational and group-based influences that shape behaviors when individuals are in the presence of others. Psychological processes enabling destructive conformity, obedience, and abuses of power became central to questions psychologists were attempting to understand regarding human behavior in the post-war period. This period also reflected significant social change and upheaval here in the United States, raising the stakes for social scientists to investigate how relationships with others, group dynamics, and power in particular influenced behaviors.

Over the summer in 1971, Zimbardo set up a makeshift prison in the basement of one of the buildings at Stanford University, randomly assigning young white males recruited to participate in this study as “inmates” or “guards.” Anticipating the potential stress that could develop from enrolling in a two-week study where an individual would potentially be incarcerated or affiliated with a “prison” as an assigned guard, Zimbardo and his team screened prospective applicants. The sample they settled on reportedly reflected the most psychologically healthy individuals of those who had applied, reflecting a group of young men most likely to withstand the potential stress of a 14-day prison simulation. He and his graduate research assistants were interested in exploring how power dynamics would influence the behaviors of participants placed in each respective role.

The results, of course, have become part of psychological lore. The interactions between the assigned prisoners and guards became so sadistic, disturbing, and cruel, that Zimbardo shut down the study after 6 days—revealing that in retrospect, he likely should have ended it even sooner. Ever the showman, even Zimbardo’s explanation for why he didn’t end the study sooner played into the narrative he had constructed regarding why the interactions between the two groups escalated to hostility so quickly: Zimbardo himself became lost in his “prison superintendent” role, losing sight that as the Principal Investigator (PI) of the experiment, his ethical responsibilities to the participants should have taken precedence

Taken in tandem with the Yale Obedience Studies conducted by Stanley Milgram in the 1960s, Zimbardo himself referred to his study as a “bookend” to such research at the time that was shedding light on the powerful role social interactions and group processes played in inciting destructive behaviors (Drury et al., 2012). The results of the study, what they reveal about group dynamics, how powerful social roles have the potential to overtake individual identity or responsibility—so many theories and themes regarding human nature (and nurture) have been dissected as a byproduct of this research.

Zimbardo himself continued to refer to this study over the course of his professional career, using it as the catalyst for other work, such as publication of his 2007 book The Lucifer Effect: Understanding How Good People Turn Evil, Ted Talks he gave on such themes as the psychology of evil, and other prominent popular cultural publications and appearances.

Fast-forward further, and American Psychologist publishes Le Texier’s (2019) scathing review of the scientific design of Zimbardo’s study, aptly titled, “Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment,” and once again, academics are revisiting this infamous study. Among many of the claims Le Texier (2019) makes based on revisiting the archives of the data collected from the study and interviewing 15 of the former 22 participants, is the “questionable scientific validity” of the results. Le Texier (2019) argues that in assigning himself the prison superintendent role, during an orientation prior to the start of the simulation, Zimbardo very explicitly demonstrated to the guards how he expected them to behave towards the inmates.

Seemingly as part of the renewed controversy over the study, National Geographic released a documentary in 2024 entitled “The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth,” which includes separate interviews with both Le Texier and Zimbardo. Filming also brings together many of the former participants of the study who had largely stayed out of the public eye, revealing resentment towards Zimbardo not only because of what they were put through as part of their participation in a study he designed, but also in how they perceive he capitalized on their suffering to craft a specific narrative regarding what the results of the study revealed.

Zimbardo categorically denies having coached assigned inmates in any way regarding the behaviors they demonstrated over the course of the study. Similarly, Le Texier maintains his previously written position by revealing in the interview he did not set out to undermine the authenticity of the study, but rather, came to such a conclusion through his investigation of archival materials from the study. Rather than answering the question of whether Le Texier’s (2019) critiques of Zimbardo’s research design were valid, the 2024 documentary poses more questions, as it is clear from watching the former participants interact with one another and reflect on the study that it did, in fact, leave a profound mark on them.

Episode 1 of this Netflix series appears to reflect on the continued controversy regarding the question of whether to trust Zimbardo’s claims from this study by presenting this simulation as “without bias.” To be clear: this most recent attempt at revisiting Zimbardo’s infamous study is in no way a scientific pursuit and entirely reality television fodder. Even with this qualifier, however, I can’t say I wasn’t compelled by what appeared to transpire in this six-episode reality TV series, dubbed as a contemporary, unscripted, redefined version of the Stanford Prison Experiment.

For my thoughts on what transpires over the course of this show—and whether it reflects any meaningful expansion regarding what we know from the original study—stay tuned for Part 2 of this article.

item.title: Accepting Our Animal Nature
item.description:
Happiness

Accepting Our Animal Nature

Our animal nature is not something we should rise above.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Since we humans are animals, we are happiest when we attune with and express our animal nature.
  • Research shows that well-being arises from activities and environments that align with animal heritage.
  • We are mental and spiritual beings too, but those aspects should be integrated with our animal nature.
  • Our animal nature is not something we should rise above, but something we should honor and express.
Source: flickr/Akane Yamada

Some humans struggle to accept the fact that we are animals. In 1860, the scientist Thomas Huxley (grandfather of the author Aldous Huxley) caused an uproar when he voiced his support for Darwin’s theory of evolution and disputed that human beings were divinely created. In response, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce enquired sarcastically whether Huxley was descended from apes through his grandmother or his grandfather. Huxley replied that he felt no shame in being descended from apes, but he would be ashamed of the bishops’ ignorance of science.

Even now, some Christians believe that human beings are superior to all other animals because only we possess souls. As a result, we will spend eternity in heaven or hell, whereas animals simply cease to exist at death. From a different perspective, some contemporary scientists suggest that there is something special about human intelligence and consciousness that elevates us above our animal cousins. We are conscious, and they aren’t—or at least, we are more intensely conscious than they are.

Throughout history, many cultures and religions have expressed ambivalence and even hostility to the animal side of our nature. The 'spirit’ and the 'flesh’ were viewed as enemies. Christian ascetics like St. Simeon Stylites and Henry de Suso put themselves through appalling torments to try to tame their physical desires and make themselves more “spiritual.” Many cultures had (and have) a repressive attitude toward sex, viewing sexual impulses as a sinful expression of our lower animal nature.

Accepting Our Animal Nature

However, there are good reasons why we should accept our animal nature and try to live in harmony with it. I would like to introduce a simple new approach to life that I call 'animalism.' The basic principle is that, since we humans are essentially animals, we are happiest when we attune with and express our animal nature. This is why we love physical activities like sports, running, swimming, and making love. It's why so many people love walking in the countryside, gardening, and preparing food. These are all activities that hark back to, and express, our animal heritage.

Research has shown that regularly practising such activities leads to greater well-being. People who garden regularly have a higher-than-average level of well-being.1 A 2023 survey of 2000 UK adults found that people who spent 20 hours or more in a green or natural space were significantly healthier and happier than average.2

In contrast, we feel least happy when we perform activities that are least connected to our animal nature. Staring at screens or immersing ourselves in TV programmes or social media may provide a short-term thrill, but in the long term, such activities make us feel restless and frustrated. Although city life can be stimulating, there are higher levels of anxiety and depression in city dwellers compared to those in the countryside.3 Researchers have coined the term ‘urban-rural happiness gap’ to describe the lower life satisfaction in cities compared to rural areas. This is a finding that holds true all over the world.4

No doubt this is partly due to the stressors of city life, such as noise and constant activity. But perhaps it is also because, as animals, we were never meant to live amidst concrete and glass, surrounded by electronic devices and metal machines. We are meant to be surrounded by trees, plants, fields, and other animal species.

Integrating the Animal and Human

You might argue that we humans are mental and spiritual beings, in a way that animals can’t aspire to. But even our spiritual nature harks back to our animal nature. Two essential aspects of spirituality are presence and mental quietness. Animals live completely in the present and do not appear to experience the incessant mental activity that afflicts us. So, in a sense, spirituality also aligns with our animal nature. And of course, presence and mental quietness are a powerful source of well-being.

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t think. Thinking can be extremely useful, helping us to organize and plan. Innumerable human achievements have arisen from our capacity for contemplation and logical thought. But as spiritual teachers like Eckhart Tolle remind us, thinking should be a faculty that we can call on when we require it. The constant associational ‘thought-chatter’ that flows through our minds is unproductive, and even harmful.

We can be rightfully proud of the human capacity for reason, and fields such as mathematics or philosophy. We can be rightfully proud of amazing expressions of human creativity such as poetry and music. But we should always remember that we are fundamentally animals and attempt to integrate our animal heritage into our lives. We should accept all our bodily instincts and processes as healthy and natural. We should ensure that we spend time in nature, and that we regularly practice ‘animalistic’ activities, like gardening, working with our hands, walking and running.

Our animal nature is not something we should rise above, but something we should honor and express.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of the “Whatever it Takes” Culture
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

The Hidden Cost of the “Whatever it Takes” Culture

When going above and beyond becomes the job.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • The most passionate employees tend to take on extra responsibility and this choice becomes an expectation.
  • Organizational citizenship behavior is the work beyond the job description that makes teams more effective.
  • Invisible acts behind the scenes drive organizational culture and sports teams, including Ted Lasso.

When fans enjoy a sports game in person or from the comfort of their homes, few think about the person who coordinated the team's travel, the producer who ensured the replay was available, the equipment manager who made sure the athletes had backup gear to perform, or the partnership coordinator who worked late to accommodate last-minute credentials.

Yet sport is built on these invisible acts.

Every industry has work that happens behind the scenes. In sport, however, there is a particular dissonance; much of the effort contributed by these supporting actors was never part of their formal job descriptions. These acts often began as examples of commitment, dedication, or, as the Journal of Applied Psychology calls it, Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Over time, however, what was once noted in a job description as “other duties as assigned” has now become expected.

The Psychology Behind the “Whatever It Takes” Mentality

Social psychologists have long studied OCB; the discretionary actions employees perform that go beyond formal job requirements and contribute to organizational effectiveness. Examples include staying late to solve an unexpected problem, helping an overwhelmed colleague, or stepping in to protect the reputation of the team.

Sports organizations often depend on these behaviors. And one reason the show Ted Lasso may resonate with so many viewers is that it has surprisingly little to do with wins and losses and more to do with the psychology of teams.

Across four seasons, record viewers watched fictitious athletes, coaches, owners, and support staff discover a truth that social psychologists have studied for decades: high-performing organizations are rarely built on talent alone. They are also built on trust, relationships, shared identity, and the often-unnoticed actions people take on behalf of one another.

In many ways, Ted Lasso illustrated something the sports industry experiences every day. The most important work is often invisible and dangerously taken for granted. The issue is not that people help. The issue is what happens when helping becomes expected. What was once extraordinary becomes ordinary. What was once appreciated becomes assumed.

The Journal of Organizational Behavior suggests that this shift can have consequences. When employees feel pressure to engage in citizenship behaviors, they may increase their OCB, but this pressure is also associated with work–family conflict, work–leisure conflict, job stress, and intentions to quit. The distinction is important: the problem is not necessarily the act of helping itself, but what happens when discretionary contribution becomes an expectation.

When Exceptional Becomes Standard

Professional sports offer a useful illustration of how exceptional practices can gradually become organizational expectations.

Consider a suite manager.

A request started with just personally managing the attendance list for a big game because the ownership group was in town. Rather than this being a one-time request, it now becomes something this employee is tasked with doing for every game, regardless of who is in town or the gravity of the game.

This process resembles what researchers in the International Journal of Project Management and Advances in Nursing Science describe as the normalization of deviance: practices that initially depart from established standards can, over time, become accepted as normal operating practice. Once a new practice is repeated without immediate negative consequences, the standard itself can gradually shift. What was once exceptional becomes the new normal.

This is, in many ways, how innovation and advancement occur. Organizations identify better ways of supporting performance, competitors adopt them, and higher standards gradually spread across the industry.

The challenge is what happens to the work required to sustain those standards.

Every new list creates additional administrative responsibilities. Every new expectation creates new forms of invisible work. The “pitch in and make it happen” mentality can encourage employees to step outside their formal roles because the game has to go on. Over time, however, those temporary acts of contribution can become permanent responsibilities without a corresponding reconsideration of workload, role boundaries, or compensation.

The Passion Trap

This is where invisible work can become problematic. Research on citizenship behaviors generally finds that they can benefit organizations. Yet when organizations become dependent on them, a paradox emerges.

The people who care the most often absorb the most extra work.

In sports, passion can mask excessive demands. Passion is one of the sports industry's greatest strengths. It can also become one of its greatest vulnerabilities. Employees stay because they love the team. They volunteer. They sacrifice. They stay late, solve problems, fill gaps, and continue saying yes because the work matters to them. They become workaholics, according to scholars from the European Sport Management Quarterly.

When employees care deeply about the organization, they may absorb additional responsibilities without questioning whether those responsibilities belong within their role. Their willingness to contribute can make organizational gaps less visible because someone is always willing to fill them. Masking role clarity, process gaps, and staffing challenges.

Research on citizenship pressure reinforces this concern. Employees can experience a distinction between choosing to contribute beyond their formal role and feeling pressured to do so. When citizenship becomes pressured rather than discretionary, the additional contribution itself can become a source of fatigue and strain.

The result is a cycle familiar to many professionals:

The reward for being dependable is often being depended upon even more.

What begins as commitment can therefore become an invisible job demand.

Over time, however, yesterday's voluntary effort can become today's expectation.

The reward for doing more is often being asked to do even more.

The “Believe” Sign and OCB

One of the most memorable symbols in Ted Lasso was the simple yellow “Believe” sign hanging in the locker room.

The sign was never simply about positive thinking. It represented a collective commitment to contributing to something bigger than oneself. Yet when organizational citizenship becomes an expectation rather than a choice, that same commitment can come at the expense of employees, as their willingness to contribute beyond their formal roles becomes an assumed obligation.

Much like the fictional professional sport team AFC Richmond, successful organizations often rely on invisible contributors who create the conditions for excellence long before the whistle blows or the quarterly reports are finalized.

If there is a lesson leaders can take from both social psychology and Ted Lasso, it may be this: A championship culture is not built solely by the people who receive the applause. It is built by the people whose contributions make the applause possible.

The challenge for leaders is not to eliminate Organizational Citizenship Behavior. It is to ensure that generosity remains a choice rather than becoming an invisible requirement of the job.

item.title: The Outlaw Within: Trauma and Toxicity in Online Games
item.description:
Trauma

The Outlaw Within: Trauma and Toxicity in Online Games

What online role-playing games reveal about the persecutors we carry within.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Toxic online spaces in video games often reveal emotional complexes in the person behind the screen.
  • Trauma can create an inner persecutor that shames and isolates; online games can be where it becomes visible.
  • MMORPGS are works of shared imagination and, approached with curiosity, can be places where depth emerges.

Massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs) are shared virtual worlds where thousands of players live alongside one another — questing, trading, forming guilds, and taking on challenges no one player could manage alone. Most have a trade chat, a public channel where players buy and sell in-game items.

Anyone who has spent time in one knows what can happen there, as it often takes on the archetypal shape of the Wild West. Merchants hawk their services, travellers look for a party to ride with, and somewhere in the virtual saloon an outlaw surfaces. The outlaw fills the online room with slurs, cruelty, extremist politics, conspiracy theories, and a contempt that would be unthinkable face to face. The sheriff (if there is one) is seemingly absent.

Some clinicians see online spaces like this and conclude that games are volatile or hollow; they're flat, lifeless screens that pull people away from depth, relationship, and soul. I understand that view, and yet I’ve come to see it differently.

Source: Photo by Makayla Larner on Unsplash

The outlaw is not always who a person is. Sometimes, it is what takes hold of them when the law is out of town. Jung (1934/1969) used the word "complex" for a charged, autonomous pattern in the psyche; when one is activated, it speaks through a person more than the person speaks through it. He also recognized, long before today’s nervous-system language, that many psychological complexes originate in emotional shock, overwhelm, and trauma (see Jung, 1934/1969).

Strip away the persona, as anonymity does, and what often remains is a complex in full possession, in the psychological rather than spiritual sense. In other words, behind the keyboard, an old wound takes the reins.

In my clinical practice, I’ve found that games rarely invent what my clients bring to them, and rather they reveal what was already there. The same game that includes a toxic public square also asks strangers to trust a healer with their lives, and has players crafting free equipment for newcomers only a few virtual feet away from the chaos. Like the wider culture they mirror, these worlds hold both cruelty and care.

Additionally, it’s worth noting that not every game culture is the same. Some MMORPGS can feel more like a village hearth rather than a frontier, where newcomers are welcomed and compassionately guided, or where there is a sense of fellowship and shared purpose by many in the game.

The persecutor within

For people harmed by others, the most relentless persecutor is often not in the public channel at all. Dr. Donald Kalsched, a Jungian analyst, has spent much of his career exploring why. He describes how, when experience is more than a person can bear, the unconscious recruits archetypal forces to protect its most vulnerable core — what he calls the “imperishable personal spirit” (soul) that exists within everyone (Kalsched, 2021, p. 444). These psychological defences organize into what he names the Self Care System, which is a core complex in the traumatized psyche (Kalsched, 2013; 2021).

This is the same kind of structure that possesses the outlaw in a trade chat, but is now turned inward. Kalsched observes that the Self Care System regulates how much feeling and memory reach consciousness, and to do so, this trauma complex attacks the capacity to feel itself (Kalsched, 2021). In this way, the protector becomes a persecutor and inner or outer tyrant: one that mocks need, punishes hope, is symbolically violent, and insists it is safer to never rely on anyone, because dependence and vulnerability are what once led to harm. Since this also operates beneath awareness, the trauma complex keeps guarding long after the original danger has passed, like a sentry who never heard the war was over.

Some of my clients have been harmed by others who discharged their own pain and sense of existential helplessness onto them. Kalsched’s work helps me understand why that harm doesn’t stay outside and the persecutor moves in. The persecutor’s voice shames before anyone else can, predicts and projects rejection, and turns a small mistake into proof of worthlessness. The emptiness, then, is rarely a product of the game itself; it is in the inner world the persecutor has hollowed out.

Games are often where this inner world becomes visible. One misstep in a group, and the inner voice can turn crueller than any stranger in the trade chat. Games can also become the trauma complex’s refuge: a place to feel competent and in control without risking emotional intimacy. While I respect the person’s ability to survive overwhelming trauma, I also recognize that walls built for protection can become suffocating.

Source: Photo by Cemrecan Yurtman on Unsplash

Is there depth and soul in MMORPGS?

Kalsched (2021) argues that trauma can hijack the imagination, bending it toward fear, grievance, harming others, and generating a world rigidly split into extremes. Yet imagination can also work the other way, toward meaning and repair. Drawing on James Hillman, Kalsched describes the imagination as the place where the human soul lives. If that is true, then games, as vast works of shared imagination, cannot be soulless by nature. So, the real question is which imagination is at work in them?

In shared group content, someone must hold the line. The tank stands between others and danger, while the healer keeps a group alive through steadiness and good will, rather than force. For someone whose inner protector has only ever known how to attack, these roles can offer a felt experience of protecting without wounding or helping without being consumed. When a client with a developmental trauma history tells me about the night they kept their group alive, or the newcomer they patiently guided, I listen closely. Something in them is rehearsing what the persecutor never learned: how to guard or tend to others in a compassionate attuned way.

The energy of the wild frontier and the hearth exist in the same world, and in the same person. Games don’t decide which one we become. However, social and online video games like MMORPGS can show us with incredible clarity which side of our psyche is holding the reins.

item.title: It's Time to Change the Way We Understand ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

It's Time to Change the Way We Understand ADHD

Focusing on emotion dysregulation could lead to more effective treatment.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Research suggests that emotion dysregulation is the root cause of ADHD.
  • This accounts for the attention and executive function symptoms commonly associated with the disorder.
  • It also helps us understand why ADHD co-presents with other mental health conditions.
  • Addressing emotion dysregulation helps us consider what treatments might be most effective.
Source: Buddha Elemental 3D / Unsplash

There is no shortage of information regarding ADHD. Instagram and TikTok are full of "experts" who talk about what ADHD is and how to manage it. But, after decades of scholarly research, those of us who regularly assess and treat ADHD can tell you something about the condition that you may not have heard before. ADHD is not only about attention deficit, and may not primarily be about attention at all.

Awais Aftab, in his article “A.D.H.D. Is Not Necessarily About Attention,” published in The New York Times, says that evidence supports the clinical approach I’ve taken for years. We need an expanded understanding of and approach to the root cause of ADHD: emotion dysregulation.

Emotion dysregulation means having trouble managing strong emotions in a way that fits the situation. While this expands our understanding of ADHD, it does explain commonly associated issues with attention and focus. Emotion regulation plays a key role in executive functioning. This means that when people cannot regulate their body movements, manage their emotions, or organize their thoughts, it's extremely difficult to focus or to sustain attention for periods of time.

Identifying emotion dysregulation as the core issue also helps us understand why so many conditions co-occur with ADHD. Emotion dysregulation is responsible for increasing anxiety, problems with anger, and mood instability. When I speak with clients about assessing and treating their ADHD, I tell them that not only are we identifying ADHD as a problem affecting their functioning, we are attempting to prevent the onset of mental health conditions that could affect their behavior, their relationships, and their ability to carry out many activities of everyday life.

Treatment for emotion dysregulation remains controversial. Many psychiatrists and psychologists believe that medication is an important part of effective treatment. Aftab’s article cites research stating that children under the age of 12 who are treated with medication improve in attention and emotion regulation, and that medication early on increases frontal lobe development.

The best results seem to occur when therapy to teach coping strategies is paired with medication, and people learn and practice the strategies while the medication is active in their system. I can attest that children seen as outpatients for therapy, whom I teach "coping skills" for self regulation, are often unable to effectively use those coping skills in real life because they either cannot remember them or their emotions escalate too quickly. Even adults diagnosed later in life have trouble establishing a regular use of strategies to prevent the expression of intense emotions, such as anger, without supportive medication. However, while children benefit from medication within the structured school environment, adult clients who were diagnosed as children often state that they don't feel the need for medication once they're finished with school.

Aside from medication and the development of coping strategies to manage intense emotions, executive function coaching is the next best intervention to pursue. Executive function includes emotional regulation, as well as attention, working memory, organization, initiating difficult or tedious tasks, and sustaining focus until the task is completed. Coaches need to have special training to work with individuals with ADHD because strategies designed for neurotypical people are often hard to acquire, and the coach needs to know how to pivot when something isn't working. Executive function coaching is often as effective or more effective than therapy for individuals with ADHD, unless there are accompanying mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression. In this case, both are recommended interventions.

I hope that more people will recognize that ADHD is a condition primarily characterized by emotion dysregulation, which can present as issues with attention and focus. This approach highlights the importance of diagnosis and treatment, because emotional regulation is also an important component of mental and physical well-being in general. It is not enough for people with ADHD to be “functional,” whether academically or professionally. They should also have the tools and support they need to manage their emotions.

item.title: Emotional Labor and the Triple Burden Facing Women of Color
item.description:
Emotional Labor

Emotional Labor and the Triple Burden Facing Women of Color

Emotional labor in households of color often extends beyond the nuclear family.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Black women have long faced a triple burden of race, gender and economic discrimination.
  • Women of color often shoulder emotional labor that extends beyond their households into their communities.
  • Navigating racism adds an invisible emotional burden to women's family and professional responsibilities.
  • Addressing emotional labor requires confronting racism and socioeconomic inequality.

Being a historian requires me to constantly examine whose version of events we have chosen to tell. Who is doing the telling, and why? In the classic narrative of women leaving the kitchen for the workforce only to return home to a "second shift," the protagonist is presumed white, middle class, and married. But for many black women, there was no choice to leave the kitchen because they were employed as paid domestics or as wage earners their families relied upon. Then went home to their own kitchen. Rinse and repeat.

By 1970, black feminists coined the term "double jeopardy" to identify discrimination based upon racial and gender identity, subsequently adding a third element of economic status to create the term "triple jeopardy." In the black community, the code around composure, tone, and dress was understood to convey judgment upon all black Americans. One managed oneself to manage another person's perception. Think about it: that’s a lot of heavy lifting. That's what emotional labor means: when you manage yourself and shape how someone feels about you, and whether or not you feel valued in return.

Being the owner of a personal services business in Los Angeles requires me to listen to my colleagues—the women of color in our professional organizing industry about how they experience our similar work lives. My discussion with women of color really moved me and opened my eyes. I have been studying and teaching about women’s history for years, most recently through the lens of emotional labor. And here was an entire layer that has been missing: emotional labor and race.

Contemporary journalist Reniqua Allen, writing in the Washington Post in 2018, underscored this dynamic in her essay, "It’s Not Just White Women: The ‘Mental Load’ Is Real for Women of Color Too." Allen explores how women of color often face a triple burden: managing traditional household emotional labor, taking on cultural translation or mediation roles (especially in immigrant families), and navigating the emotional toll of racism in both personal and professional spheres.

I remarked on this triple burden at a talk recently. In a packed room of women of color, nodding heads all around, and shouts of "tell it!" resonated.

Emotional labor in households of color often extends beyond the nuclear family. Intergenerational caregiving is not uncommon. Taking responsibility for community affairs is another way the mental load of emotional labor extends far beyond the home. And always, families of color manage the emotional work of navigating systemic racism. In a recent interview with members of Ebony and Orderly, Professional Organizers of Color member Carolyn Rogers notes:

As women, we tend to take on the happiness of our family meaning dealing with and trying to shape the emotions of our spouse, our partner, our kids, to be sure everybody is happy in the house. So that means I have to know what's going on with them. What do they have to deal with that comes from out in the world including dealing with social issues, dealing with racial issues, dealing with how people feel about what's going on in politics, dealing with all of that. For example, my nephew lives with us. In addition to teaching him how to maneuver around the house I also pay attention to how he maneuvers in the world and how he handles things that come his way. So as women of color we are always asking the question did this bad thing happen to me because this person was just an a***hole in general or it only happened to me because I'm a brown person. There is an additional aspect when you put race into the picture in addition to the regular everyday stuff.

Professional Organizer Robyn Reynolds says: “Picture this. I arrive early to a mostly affluent neighborhood just to be sure I am on time and haven’t gotten lost, plus I like to be early! So, here I am, a Black woman sitting in her car for sometimes up to 20 minutes. While I know that I have a reason to be there, others may not. So far, I have not had the cops called on me but it is something I think about often. Will today be the day? Then, the time has come for me to ring the bell and meet my client for the first time. Unless they have looked at my website, they do not know that I am a person of color. For some it is surprising, for others it doesn’t matter. The point is that I never know whether or not they care.”

Arlie Hochschild, the originator of the term ‘emotional labor’ extends the concept of emotional management to racial reconciliation, noting that:

“…a Black person may be treated as a ‘representative’ of all black people…Or in other ways, people of color and really minorities of every sort, face the task of peeling off other people’s projections onto them…Any member of a minority, whether based on gender, sexuality, religion, disability…is tacitly given the extra emotional task of helping others relate to oneself in a relaxed and accepting way.”

Dr. Belinda Tucker, UCLA Professor Emerita of Psychiatry and Behavioral Science, notes that she and her husband worked hard to create together an environment at home where he was able to express feelings related to the systemic racism rampant in his workplace. “We uplift and elevate masculinity because it's so brought down by the man outside. Back in the day when I did my graduate research, the comment ‘Well, I want to uplift and elevate my husband so that he feels like a man,’ might have elicited from me a white-privileged response like “Get counseling.” But now I get it. Racism still reigns in this country, so a black woman saying the same thing, I think, “Oh, okay,” because I understand the context is so different.

There is a cost to carrying the weight of emotional labor. Referred to as the “superwoman schema" – many among us feel compelled to demonstrate unwavering competence. We suppress our feelings. We don’t like feeling vulnerable and we tend to go beyond the mark, over and above, accomplishing feats amid limitation. We deny self-care in our ongoing care for others. Exhausted and depressed, women “crash out,” a term used in a 2025 article by Miriam Musa in Rolling Out, a digital magazine for people of color, phenomena for women of color shouldering complex emotional labor differs from typical burnout. A 2025 article by Miriam Musa in Rolling Out, a digital magazine for people of color, notes that “The crash out trend has highlighted how much unpaid emotional and domestic labor black women perform in their families, workplaces and communities. This invisible work includes managing household logistics, supporting colleagues, mentoring younger people, and maintaining family relationships. It represents significant economic value that goes unrecognized… the ripple effects show just how much others depend upon their unacknowledged contributions.”

For these reasons, when creating the revised 2nd Edition of Emotional Labor, Judith Kolberg and I sought to document the experience of woman of color. Emotional labor transcends housewife problems and cannot be solved with better chore charts alone. Emotional labor has just as much to do with racism and socioeconomic status as it does femininity. Recognizing emotional labor means addressing its source, thereby enabling individuals to distribute it equitably among household members and partners.

item.title: When Your Employer Collapses, What's Next for You?
item.description:
Career

When Your Employer Collapses, What's Next for You?

How to navigate job loss, activate your network, and protect your career.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • You can be indispensable at work and still lose your job overnight.
  • The most dependable employees may be the least prepared for an unexpected job loss.
  • Our employer's prestigious reputation offers less career security than you might think.
Weil, Gotshal & Manges is shutting down, causing thousands to lose their jobs.
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

Weil, Gotshal & Manges, a nearly century-old global law firm with 1,200 lawyers and more than two billion dollars in annual revenue, announced their plans to wind down operations. A few dominos set this cascade in motion. Prominent partners were poached and moved to other firms. Traditionally, clients follow them. But the firm still has high fixed costs. Subsequent merger discussions failed, and the firm’s leadership recommended dissolving the firm, pending a partnership vote.

For thousands of lawyers, paralegals, administrative professionals and other staff members, their life is in upheaval. They worked hard, consistently delivered results, nurtured relationships, and believed they had a secure future with the firm. Overnight, that changed.

Like many who have been let go, a certain realization hits home. You can be indispensable to your employer, and still be professionally vulnerable.

The lessons from the dissolution of a prominent law firm can teach us many lessons, both for those who are facing an unexpected career disruption and those who feel they are comfortably employed.

Short-Term Response: Regain Control

1. Make your invisible work visible.

Too often, high performers become what I call the Office Mechanic (read my Psychology Today article on this). They are the people who prevent a crisis, solve problems, and keep the organization functioning. They absorb many stressors so the people above them in the hierarchy don’t need to. Their work is often done in the shadows. They are so reliable that people barely notice what they’ve done. Because of them, there's no fire, no drama, and no one notices.

If this describes you, keep a log of problems you solved, disasters you prevented, and ways your work improved. Don’t worry about going back to the beginning of your career. Start with the last three problems you solved, or the last twelve months. Without disclosing confidential information, use quantitative impact measures. Use percentages, dollar signs, and greater/less than indicators. Show impact. These become the stories you share with others and post on your LinkedIn. They go beyond what you did to the impact you had.

2. Activate your network strategically.

Panicked emails rarely work, especially if you are sending generic mass messages saying “I am looking for a new opportunity.” Instead, make a list of five people who know the quality of your work, five who are connected to organizations you respect, and three who could or would advocate for you.

Contact them with a specific request. Don’t just say “I need help finding a new job.” That is too vague. Instead, ask for introductions to specific people or types of people. You want the person to picture in their mind who they should reach out to on your behalf. You can also inquire about insight into an industry, or recommendations for specific opportunities. The more detailed you can be, the better. The goal is to turn relationships into conversations and conversations into opportunities.

3. Convert praise into advocacy.

If you’ve ever received praise at work (read my PT article about why this might be a dead end), such as “You’re the glue that keeps us together” or “We’d be lost with you,” you might be recognized for your performance but overlooked for advancement.

Consider three people who have called you exceptional in one form or another. Reach out to them and ask them to recommend you, introduce you to specific people, or serve as references. Again, be specific in your ask.

Being appreciated feels wonderful but being advocated for is what opens doors.

Long-Term Response: Build Career Resilience

4. Never build your career around one person.

Too often, people join an organization for the opportunity to work with an influential leader. Assuming they ever get face time with that person, that leader can leave, retire, or lose influence overnight, leaving you as collateral damage.

Protect yourself by building a mentoring team with relationships across departments, organizations, and industries. Ask yourself this critical question: If my boss disappeared tomorrow, who else would know my value?

5. Recalibrate your network before you need it.

You might be so good at keeping your head down and doing your job well that you’ve neglected your network. Many successful professionals have deep internal networks and surprisingly weak external ones. Meaning, you are known within your organization or industry, and invisible outside of it.

To combat this, be proactive. Every quarter, reconnect with three people outside your organization. Consider sending a non-committal email during holidays, such as Thanksgiving, New Year, or Fourth of July. Develop relationships with people who can challenge your thinking, expand your perspective, and introduce you to new opportunities, and be sure to keep in touch with them, especially when you don’t need their help.

Your employer's prestigious name may open doors, which is known as your social proof. However, your professional reputation must survive independently of it. Your social proof should launch you, not carry you.

Share your expertise, develop transferable skills, and ensure that people beyond your immediate colleagues understand the problems you solve. Routinely, offer to help others, before you ever ask for help in return. Even if you are out of work, take the time to continuously uplevel your skills. Consider online courses such as those available through LinkedIn Learning — free with a US library card.

Weil's employees are facing tremendous uncertainty, which is likely extremely unsettling. Their experience should remind everyone that organizational prestige and individual excellence cannot eliminate career risk. Prepare accordingly.

The ultimate career security is knowing that your skills, relationships, reputation, and opportunities can travel with you, even when your employer cannot.

item.title: Who Decides Whether Someone Is Mentally Capable of Voting?
item.description:
Law and Crime

Who Decides Whether Someone Is Mentally Capable of Voting?

Examining the voting rights of people with mental illness or cognitive impairment

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • People with mental health conditions or cognitive impairments generally retain the right to vote.
  • States may restrict voting rights based on legally established mental incapacity.
  • Caregivers and mental health professionals can help individuals exercise their voting rights.

Voting is a fundamental right in free and democratic societies (Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, 2026). The Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution provide important safeguards against arbitrary and discriminatory restrictions on voting rights. But what happens when individuals have schizophrenia, cognitive impairment, bipolar disorder, uncontrolled addiction, or other mental health disorders that may compromise their decision-making capacity? What does the law say about their right to vote, and who has the authority to determine when that right may be restricted?

Relevant Laws

Various federal and state laws protect voting rights, including those of people with mental health conditions or cognitive impairments. Under the Voting Rights Act (1965), individuals with disabilities who need assistance voting have the right to receive help from a person of their choice, subject certain exceptions (e.g., not an employer). For instance, someone with an anxiety disorder, cognitive impairment, autism, or other mental health condition that makes voting difficult may ask a friend or family member to assist them (Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, 2026). The Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) also prohibits discrimination by state and local government officials, including individuals responsible for administering elections (U.S. Department of Justice, 2024). For example, election officials generally cannot prohibit voters with disabilities from bringing trained service animals into polling places. States cannot enact laws that discriminate against people with disabilities (Doe v. Rowe, 2001), for instance, disqualifying people from voting simply because they have a mental illness.

Under the National Voter Registration Act (1993), states may remove individuals from voter registration rolls based on mental incapacity, as provided by state law. However, states differ in whether and how they determine whether someone lacks the mental capacity to vote. For instance, Florida Statute § 97.041 prohibits individuals who have been adjudicated mentally incapacitated with respect to voting from voting unless their voting rights have been restored. New Mexico’s Constitution (Article VII, § 1) permits restrictions based on mental incapacity only when individuals cannot mark their ballots and cannot communicate their voting preferences. In contrast, California Elections Code § 2208 presumes that individuals retain the right to vote even when they have court-appointed conservators. Voting rights may be removed only following a specific court ruling, supported by clear and convincing evidence, that the individual cannot communicate a desire to participate in voting, even with reasonable accommodations.

Bottom Lines

Although voting laws vary from state to state, the following general principles apply across the United States:

  1. Mental health diagnoses do not automatically disqualify people from voting. Individuals do not lose their voting rights simply because they have a mental health condition, cognitive impairment, or intellectual disability, or because they take medication for a mental health condition.
  2. Voting rights may be restricted based on legal determinations of mental incapacity. In states permitting such restrictions, individuals may lose their voting rights through a court determination or other legally authorized process. These restrictions must comply with constitutional and federal disability-rights protections (Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, 2026).
  3. Guardianship or hospitalization does not necessarily mean losing the right to vote. In many states, individuals retain their voting rights even when a court appoints a guardian to assist them with personal, financial, or healthcare decisions, or when they have been admitted to a mental health facility. The specific laws and court orders governing voting rights vary from state to state.
  4. Election officials must provide reasonable accommodations for voters with disabilities. This may include allowing individuals with mental health conditions or cognitive impairments to receive assistance from someone of their choice, subject to certain legal exceptions.
  5. Voting decisions belong to the voter. Individuals should not be prevented from voting simply because family members, mental health professionals (MHPs), caregivers, or others disagree with their political views or preferred candidates. Likewise, people providing voting assistance must respect the voter's choices rather than substitute their own preferences.

A recent Wisconsin Supreme Court decision illustrates the importance of protecting the privacy of individuals whose voting rights have been restricted due to mental incapacity. In Wisconsin Voter Alliance v. Secord (2026), the court ruled that records identifying individuals who had been adjudicated incompetent to vote were confidential under state guardianship laws and were not subject to public disclosure. Protecting privacy also fits with the ethics of mental health professionals, which includes respecting patient’s right to confidentiality (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; NASW, 2021).

Roles of Family, Friends, Caregivers, and Mental Health Professionals

Family members, friends, caregivers, and mental health professionals (MHPs) can play vital roles in helping individuals with mental health conditions or cognitive impairments exercise their right to vote. First, they can explore whether individuals are interested in voting and identify what assistance they may need to participate. This may include providing information about voter registration, early or mail-in voting, sample ballots, candidates’ positions and policies, and transportation options for getting to polling places (e.g., public transportation, rides from family or friends). For state-by-state voting guides, see https://www.aapd.com/voter-info.

If individuals experience anxiety or distress related to voting, supporters can help them identify ways to manage these concerns, such as voting by mail or using relaxation and breathing exercises. When individuals encounter barriers to voting (e.g., inaccessible polling booths, ballots that are difficult to read or understand), family members, MHPs, and others can help them advocate for reasonable accommodations and resolve accessibility concerns. While providing assistance with the voting process, supporters should respect individuals’ autonomy, ensuring that assistance facilitates their own voting decisions rather than influencing or substituting the preferences of others.

Generally, MHPs and other supporters are not legally required to assist individuals with mental health conditions or cognitive impairments in exercising their right to vote. Nevertheless, providing voting assistance may be an ethical or moral responsibility, reflecting respect for individuals’ dignity, worth, autonomy, and right to participate in democratic processes. Professional ethical standards for counselors, psychologists, and social workers emphasize respect for clients’ autonomy and self-determination (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; Barsky, 2023; NASW, 2021). These principles support respecting and facilitating clients’ right to vote, should they wish to exercise it.

When individuals appear to lack the mental capacity to make informed voting decisions, supporters should not automatically assume that they have lost their right to vote. Instead, they can explore whether reasonable accommodations or supported decision-making could help individuals express their own voting preferences. For instance, some people with dementia experience greater mental clarity in the morning and increased confusion or cognitive difficulties later in the day, a phenomenon known as sundowning. For these individuals, arranging to vote in the morning, when they are more alert and better able to express their preferences, may be helpful. If individuals cannot communicate their voting preferences, even with appropriate assistance, supporters should refrain from making voting choices on their behalf.

If someone is coercing, intimidating, or manipulating a vulnerable adult to influence their voting decisions, this may constitute unlawful interference with their voting rights (Voting Rights Act, 1965). Depending on the circumstances and applicable state laws, such conduct may also raise concerns about abuse or exploitation that warrant reporting to adult protective services or election authorities (e.g., Florida Statutes, 2026, § 415.1034).

Conclusion

Having a mental health condition or cognitive impairment is not, in itself, a legal justification to restrict a person’s right to vote. Although voting rights may be restricted under certain state laws when individuals are legally determined to lack the capacity to vote, such restrictions must comply with constitutional, federal, and state protections. Family members, friends, MHPs, and other supporters can play important roles in helping individuals exercise their voting rights, including providing appropriate assistance and accommodations. They should also remain vigilant against exploitation, coercion, and discrimination, while respecting each individual’s autonomy, dignity, and right to participate in the democratic process.

item.title: My Kid Has Another Group Project With Some Not-So-Great Kids
item.description:
Parenting

My Kid Has Another Group Project With Some Not-So-Great Kids

Group projects can be a valuable tool for learning group skills.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Resilient kids learn to function in groups when some peers are poor participants.
  • School group projects teach lifetime skills of tolerance, managing expectations, and self-sacrifice.
  • No perfect group exists and no kid is a perfect group participant, including your child.

When my teachers announced a group project, I used to worry about who my group members would be. What if they didn’t do their part? What if they were bad students who didn’t care and brought down the group grade?

When my kids were in school, I found myself reliving the same dilemma: I'd listen to one kid complain about other students' lack of helpful input or worry about how my academically challenged kid would affect the group's morale or grade. If I am honest, I wouldn’t have wanted him assigned to my group!

As a therapist, I have had many sessions with kids, teens, and adults who have suffered great anxiety and interpersonal distress because someone else in a group was not able to function effectively, whether it was for school, sports, work, or an organization. I have also seen how easy it is for parents to respond to this dilemma by asking that their child be assigned to a more favorable group, especially if they are on the receiving end of their child’s anxiety and anger when a group project is compromised by a troublesome peer. This seems like a great thing to do, right? Unfortunately, this is a misguided way to help your kid, even if it is well-intentioned. Let me explain.

Think about how often you have to work in groups or deal with groups in your work and private life. Even if you deliberately avoid joining boards or leadership groups, you likely participate in other groups, with neighbors, parent organizations, volunteers, your family, friends, or work colleagues. They almost always include some effective group members and those who are less effective or even detrimental. As someone with a long history of leading and belonging to many groups, I cannot think of a single situation where everyone consistently did what served the group or its purpose, including me! This means that the problem your child faces is not finding the perfect group, which is humanly impossible, but figuring out how to function well in any group.

What if you framed each school group project as part of the long-term learning process of being a group member and/or a group leader with imperfect peers? Instead of trying to isolate your child from the learning process for the sake of grades, what if you embraced the struggle to learn how to manage expectations for oneself and others, to figure out how to compensate for those who are not as skilled, willing, or engaged, and to learn how to sacrifice for the greater good of the group? Aren’t these abilities you wish for your child? When you send the message that it is unacceptable to work with those who don’t share your skills or values, you risk making it harder for your child to become an adult who can live in harmony with those who are different. You risk contributing to cancel culture.

If you take this long-term view of group projects, then it means you should try to do the following:

  1. First, agree with your child’s distress when they complain: “Yes, it stinks when someone did not do their part in the group presentation. That is really unfair and annoying.” This validates their experience.
  2. Normalize their experience by pointing out past circumstances of typical group dysfunction and eventual recovery. Share your own similar group experiences and explain how your life continued, whether or not the group was successful.
  3. Remind them of the bigger goal: to learn how to identify what each group member is capable of and then to redesign the tasks around realistic expectations. For example: “If that kid won’t do any research, then why not have everyone else do the research?”
  4. Ask them to give compassion to the students who are not able to participate to their satisfaction: “If they never do their homework, then why would you expect them to do group work? They have not yet learned how to do school.” This means you should never vilify the kids who cannot fulfill the group mission, just like you would never vilify the benchwarmers in kids’ sports.
  5. Remind your kid there is no perfect group, just some kids who figure out faster how much can be accomplished when they learn how to work well in a group. Your kid needs to learn that group effort is priceless for society to function well, even when some members can't be effective in groups.

item.title: Reality Becoming Too Much for You? Crack Open a Fantasy Book
item.description:
Fantasies

Reality Becoming Too Much for You? Crack Open a Fantasy Book

Reading fantasy can offer a temporary, healthy escape from the real world.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Fantasy books can offer a temporary escape from everyday stress.
  • Reading for pleasure can support relaxation and self-exploration.
  • Escapism can be restorative when it is not about long-term avoidance.
  • Reading doesn’t need to be about self-improvement; sometimes a good story is enough.
Source: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels

Browse any bookstore, and you are bound to see a bevy of covers featuring dragons, fairies, warrior princesses, and brave Hobbit travelers. The fantasy book market is red-hot, projected to reach $26 billion by 2033 and seemingly growing faster than any other genre. The latest book in author Sarah J. Maas’s hit “ACOTAR” series, for example, A Court of Splintered Harmony, quickly rose to the number 2 spot on Amazon leading up to its release on October 27, 2026, and saw bookstores across the U.S. selling out of copies for midnight release parties.

With these statistics, one has to wonder whether the popularity of fantasy novels has anything to do with people desperately trying to escape our current reality.

Since the dawn of modern literature, fantasy tropes such as damsels in distress, fantastical flying beasts, and dragon-slayers have been popular fodder for writers. Escapism has always been a reason people turn to books. Today, people may feel they have all the more reason to turn to fantasy novels as the laundry piles up, the email inbox begins to overflow, and back-and-forth political ads dominate daily TV watching. Somehow, reading about a kingdom on the brink of destruction or a powerful huntress on a mission to save her village starts to sound relaxing in comparison.

So what is it about fantasy books that allows people to lean into escapism, and is it a healthy way to deal with a reality that may feel all too “real” sometimes?

Getting lost in a book

Many of us have experienced the thrill of becoming so engrossed in a book that the outside world seems to melt away. The attention to detail, the emotion contained within the prose, and the mental imagery are enough to transport us to another place and time. This sense can be heightened with fantasy novels.

Reading gives us some place to go, if just for a moment. Through reading fantasy, we can become emotionally invested in moments that do not require us to upend our daily lives. There can be great appeal to this temporary escape, especially for people who have a lot going on in the real world. While the fire-breathing dragon may be terrifying, it’s not waiting for your email response.

In one study, one in three respondents said books offered the best form of escapism from a bad day, illustrating that books may not only be a fun form of entertainment, but could be important for overall mental wellness.

Fantasy books offer an enticing doorway to escapism and more

There is nothing more far removed from modern life than a fantasy novel, yet they still offer familiar feelings within those fantastical settings. There’s love, friendship, fear, grief, belonging, and responsibility woven into fantasy stories—feelings that most people can relate to. Fantasy novels give us a peek into what is possible outside of everyday roles. While we may not be able to ride upon a winged horse or consort with fairies, we can embrace friendship or take a chance on new adventures, just like the people in our favorite books.

According to studies, reading for pleasure can support feelings of relaxation, give us new perspectives, enhance empathic abilities, reawaken memories, or give us a better sense of self-understanding. Even for fantasy readers, a story can feel very close to their own lives while still giving them something fun and imaginative to indulge in.

That being said, giving in to the escapism provided by fantasy novels doesn’t necessarily mean that you are actively avoiding your real life. What matters in fantasy reading is how the activity serves you. People want to enjoy a stopover in a fantasy world and then return feeling refreshed, and often that can come with a new perspective on life. This is different from an approach of wanting to stay perpetually distracted so that one never has to face the reality of their current situation.

Readers may want to stop and think about what they get out of their fantasy reading and whether they may find themselves indulging in it more as daily tasks and responsibilities fall by the wayside. When readers take the time to be thoughtful about how reading fits into their lives, escapism can be more about pleasure than detrimental avoidance.

Still, sometimes a book is just a book: a fun escape from the day-to-day doldrums so many of us face. Fantasy novels are there to entertain, and not every enjoyable activity needs to include a pathway to self-improvement. Sometimes, people just need to admit they like spending some time reading about the adventures of fairy warriors, dragon slayers, and trolls.

The useful question when we look at fantasy novel escapism is what that time away from the real world makes possible for us when we return. But in the meantime, we all may need to embrace the idea that sometimes the laundry can wait—at least for one more chapter.

item.title: Three Tips to Teach Your Child Emotional Intelligence
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

Three Tips to Teach Your Child Emotional Intelligence

Emotional intelligence is learned at home, long before anyone teaches it.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional intelligence is largely learned at home from parents who notice and respond to feelings.
  • You cannot teach your child a skill no one ever taught you, which is how low emotional intelligence repeats.
  • Paying attention, feeling with your child, and responding to feelings are three things you can start now.
  • This is not about being a perfect parent. The effort itself is what your child receives.
Source: Mediaphotos / AdobeStock

Nora’s daughter came home from school feeling sad. A friend had not saved her a seat at lunch, and it all came out at the kitchen table.

“That’s not worth getting upset about,” Nora told her. “You’ll sit together tomorrow.”

Her daughter stopped talking about it and took her homework upstairs. Nora went on with her day, relieved that her daughter’s tears had passed.

Nothing in that exchange looks harmful, and that’s what makes it so invisible.

Do you ever respond to your child as Nora did?

If so, you are in very good company. As a psychologist who has specialized in childhood emotional neglect for years, I have watched this way of managing a child’s feelings pass quietly from one generation to the next.

Emotional intelligence (EI) is your ability to manage and understand emotions and relationships, your own as well as others’. I have observed that it is more vital to life success and satisfaction than general intelligence. This makes EI a very important skill for parents to teach their children.

The good news: children automatically learn EI when they are raised by parents who have it themselves. Parents with EI are able to understand what their child is feeling and why. Their emotionally attuned responses to the child model and teach them how to read, understand, and respond to their own and others’ feelings in a healthy way (Zinsser et al., 2021).

The bad news: a parent who struggles with EI themselves may lack the skills necessary to be able to teach them to their child. In other words, you can’t teach your child what you don’t know. This is how low EI automatically trickles down through generations of families.

Childhood Emotional Neglect

One way to be sure you don’t teach your child about emotion is to simply ignore their emotions while you are raising them, like the example of Nora above. That is childhood emotional neglect. It’s not about what you do to your child. It’s about what you do not do for them.

If, often enough, you seem not to notice that your child is upset, sad, angry, hurt, or anxious, you are subtly telling them that their sadness, anger, pain, or anxiety don’t matter. You are teaching them to ignore their own feelings.

Emotionally neglected children grow up to experience a variety of challenges, only one of which is low emotional intelligence. As adults, these children also struggle with excessive guilt and self-blame, feelings of emptiness, and a general lack of joy in life.

If you see yourself in that, please know it’s not your fault. When feelings go unnoticed in a home, no one growing up there learns how emotions work, and that may simply be what happened to you.

No loving parent wants to set their child up for that scenario. But parenting is probably the most complicated job in the world. In fact, it is built into the natural process of parenting that even the most loving parents will pass their own strengths and weaknesses on to their children. Often, the only way to stop that cycle is to consciously make the effort to override it.

Three Things to Start Doing

1. Pay attention. Work hard to see your child’s true nature. What does your child like, dislike, get angry about, feel afraid of, or struggle with? Feed these observations back to your child in a non-judgmental way so that your child can see themselves through your eyes and feel how well you know them.

Life advantage: Your child will see themselves reflected in your eyes, and they will know who they are. They will realize that, no matter their strengths and weaknesses, they are lovable, and they are enough. This will give them confidence in their life choices and will make them resilient to life’s challenges.

2. Feel an emotional connection to your child. Strive to feel what your child is feeling (empathy), whether you agree with it or not. When you feel your child’s emotion, they will feel an instant bond with you.

Life advantage: Your child will learn empathy and will have healthier relationships throughout their life.

3. Respond competently to your child’s emotional needs. Do not judge your child’s feelings as right or wrong. Look beyond the feeling to the source. Help your child name their emotion. Help them manage the emotion.

Life advantage: Your child will have a healthy relationship with their own emotions. They will naturally know that their feelings are important and how to put them into words and manage them.

If those three tips describe something you did not receive yourself, do not despair. You can learn all this now, at the same time your child does. Start by noticing your own feelings and putting words to them. The more you do that for yourself, the more naturally you will do it for your child.

It Is Not About Perfection

No parent can follow these tips perfectly, of course. This is not about perfection; it’s about making the effort. Effort in itself shows love and care. When your child sees you trying to understand their feelings or feel their feelings, whether you succeed or not, they receive a powerful message: Your feelings matter to me.

And what your child will hear: You matter. They will internalize this valuable knowledge that will empower them for all of their life.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.
