item.title: OCD in Men: The Disturbing Thoughts They're Afraid to Share
item.description:
OCD

OCD in Men: The Disturbing Thoughts They're Afraid to Share

Men with OCD often have very alarming symptoms, making diagnosis difficult.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Men with OCD more often experience intrusive thoughts about harm, sex, or religion.
  • Shame and fear of judgment can keep men from disclosing their obsessive thoughts.
  • When doctors misunderstand these symptoms, misdiagnosis can lead to years without treatment.
  • Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is just as effective for men as it is for women.

When someone mentions OCD, what’s the first image to pop into your mind? Washing your hands too many times, perhaps, or repeatedly checking the oven before you go to bed? These common notions aren’t inaccurate, but unfortunately they show only one side of what’s actually quite a multifarious disorder: they’re the symptoms that occur most commonly in women. By contrast, men experience OCD in very different ways: their obsessive thoughts and repetitive behaviors don’t focus as often on themes of contamination, but instead on violence, sex, or religious blasphemy (to name a few). And this gender discrepancy creates other problems, too, making the experience of OCD a unique challenge for many men.

Source: Image generated by ChatGPT

Broadly, the diagnosis of OCD shows huge differences according to sex: men are much more often misdiagnosed than women. Last year’s analysis by the International OCD Foundation (Deusser, 2025) found that nearly twice as many women as men had received an OCD diagnosis. The study went on to conclude that the inconsistency couldn’t be explained by the disorder itself, which doesn’t discriminate by sex. Neither was it due to any failure to seek help by OCD sufferers (as a study by Wongbusarakum et al. found in 2025). Instead, the gender difference in OCD incidence appears to be caused by a bias in the way men and women are diagnosed. To put it plainly, the OCD symptom constellations occurring most often in men are harder for their doctors to recognize, so the diagnosis is often not applied. Men with OCD then end up living with the disorder for a long time before it’s recognized: according to the IOCDF, delays between the onset of men’s symptoms and the establishment of a diagnosis often last as long as seven years, and can even go as high as seventeen — meaning that a large number of men end up struggling alone with their symptoms for over a decade.

As I noted above, OCD more often presents differently in men. According to a 2019 study in Current Psychiatry Reports, while women more frequently experience obsessions related to contamination, men tend to obsess over the possibility of doing harm to others, transgressing sexual boundaries, or behaving in ways that their religions would condemn. The symptoms reported by men with OCD generally focus more narrowly, as well, while women present for evaluation with more wide-ranging obsessions and compulsions (Mathes et al., 2019). This means that men are more likely than women to be deeply tormented by their intrusive thoughts without showing obvious compulsive behaviors. For example, they may worry constantly about causing harm to people they care about, but then compulsively perform internal, thought-based rituals — that are very difficult for others to notice — to defuse that anxiety. And also, if the men coping with thoughts and fears like these do not understand that they are experiencing the symptoms of a well-understood disorder, they may instead begin to believe they are bad or immoral people. These fears, too, may cause delays in the search for appropriate treatment, or the assignment of a correct diagnosis.

The powerful and repeated unacceptable thoughts I have mentioned can comprise the least obvious, most stigmatized form of OCD. Unacceptable-thought OCD (sometimes called UT-OCD) is far more likely than contamination-based OCD to be wrongly identified; Coles et al. (2023) reported that these recurring thoughts were wrongly diagnosed (as something other than OCD) at a rate of 59.9% — in contrast to contamination OCD, which was only misidentified 27.1% of the time. Moreover, because intrusive thoughts about causing harm or acting out sexually are also the most highly stigmatized by others, misdiagnoses such as paraphilia or psychosis can themselves cause significant, additional psychological distress. Obsessions over one’s sexual orientation, which can be powerfully unsettling, also occur in men more often than in women (Williams & Farris, 2011). These intrusive thoughts, too, can be deeply shameful, which places further obstacles in the path of seeking help.

Another layer of complexity, over and above the challenge of disclosing these thoughts and feelings, also works to silence men with OCD: our society’s cultural norms for masculinity. Men are traditionally expected to be strong in generic ways — self-reliant and stoic — which means that asking for help, or even admitting to themselves that something might be wrong, can seem “unmanly.” One of the biggest barriers to treatment, according to a 2024 article in the British Journal of Clinical Psychology, is the shame generated by this perceived lack of masculinity. Worse, the disorder of OCD is exacerbated by the secrecy and avoidance caused by shame; men feeling this way, the thinking goes, are less likely to confront their own intrusive thoughts. Some of them will fear being rejected by their friends and families if their intrusive thoughts were to become public, and the only apparent solution may be to hide these thoughts away — making it impossible to disconfirm them. Similarly, if men cannot tell their doctors the truth about their thoughts, they won’t get appropriate treatment. What results from this interaction between shame and avoidance is a doubling-down of the disorder: if untreated, OCD’s intrusive thoughts and compensatory behaviors get worse, which creates more shame, which in turn redoubles the avoidance.

Of course, the picture isn’t completely hopeless; the good news is that OCD treatment outcomes show no significant differences according to gender (Mathes et al., 2019). Therapy for OCD, which usually involves a controlled exposure to anxiety-producing stimuli coupled with the prevention of the patient’s avoidant or anxiety-neutralizing behaviors, works just as well for men as it does for women. Exposure and response prevention (or ERP, as it is known), means gaining through experience the knowledge that one’s thoughts do not perfectly represent one’s intentions, and that the distress one may feel when experiencing intrusive violent or sexual images actually means one is less likely to act out those thoughts. (One of my old supervisors often said he would trust his OCD patients with his life, as they were the people who expressed the most concern over protecting others.) People who suffer from OCD, no matter their gender, stand to benefit a great deal — and to overcome a lot of suffering — if they can find a way to seek treatment despite their fears and feelings of shame.

Men with unacceptable-thought OCD may believe they are awful human beings; they may hide their symptoms from the people in their life; they may suffer in silence for years. But if mental health clinicians can learn to better recognize the atypical presentation of UT-OCD, the gap in diagnosis may begin to change — and just the same, if men can learn to challenge conventions about traditionally masculine stoicism and cut down on the shame that increases the intensity and harm of OCD, this obstacle to treatment can also be minimized. If you recognize yourself in these descriptions of unacceptable-thought OCD, no matter how distressing it has been to you, I earnestly encourage you to find a way to talk to someone you trust.

item.title: When Is the Best Time to Start Your Child's ADHD Meds?
item.description:
ADHD

When Is the Best Time to Start Your Child's ADHD Meds?

The age when a child starts on ADHD medication affects brain chemistry.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Medication-naïve children with ADHD have lower brain iron content, as compared to peers.
  • Starting psychostimulant treatment earlier, rather than later, was associated with more brain iron.
  • The elevated brain iron levels were associated with increased dopamine function and reduced symptoms.

This is a story about iron: What does it do in the brain, and why should someone with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) care?

ADHD is a common neurodevelopmental disorder in school-age children and adolescents. The disorder is characterized by inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. It can cause individuals to have significant challenges with everyday tasks and social interactions.

In my opinion, as a neuroscientist who specializes in brain chemistry, the underlying cause of such a complex psychiatric condition should never be distilled into the dysfunction of a single neurotransmitter system. For example, neuroscientists now realize that psychosis is not a problem with the health of dopamine neurons and that depression has very little to do with serotonin neuronal activity. (To learn more, click here.) Gross oversimplifications of the underlying mechanisms of these disorders have greatly slowed the discovery of effective therapies for them.

With these cautions in mind, let’s examine the role of iron in the function of dopamine neurons in the brains of children with ADHD.

Reduced activity of the brain’s dopamine neurons is thought to play a significant role in the pathophysiology of ADHD. This is why psychostimulants that increase the activity of dopamine neurons, and the subsequent release of dopamine within a small number of brain regions, have become the primary treatment for ADHD symptoms. The existing logic supporting this conclusion is that if increasing dopamine release reduces symptoms, then the symptoms of ADHD are due to too little release of dopamine somewhere in the brain.

Are ADHD meds that increase the release of dopamine from dopamine neuronal terminals effective?

Yes, ADHD medications are effective, usually within the first hour after taking the drugs, in reducing core symptoms like inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, improving focus, behavior, and daily functioning (Parlatini et al., 2024).

How does iron play a role?

Brain iron found inside dopamine neurons controls the enzyme that leads to the synthesis of dopamine. It’s considered the rate-limiting step. People with iron‑deficiency anemia who do not absorb enough iron from their diet do not produce adequate amounts of dopamine. If the deficiency is severe, anemics may experience reduced motivation, poor concentration, and mood changes typical of someone with reduced dopamine production. As expected, in the brain, iron levels are high in regions that contain lots of dopamine neurons. New magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques can provide estimates of brain iron levels. Under normal circumstances, the iron content of dopamine-rich brain regions rapidly increases throughout childhood and adolescence and is associated with the maturation of dopamine neurons.

Medication-naïve children with ADHD have lower brain iron content. MRI studies show that ADHD children given psychostimulants have higher brain iron content than medication-naïve children with ADHD. Furthermore, their brain iron content was similar to that of neurotypical children without ADHD. In addition, longer duration of psychostimulant treatment was associated with higher levels of iron. The elevated levels of iron have a functional consequence. Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that long-term treatment with standard psychostimulants directly increases dopamine function in the brain of children with ADHD (Kaminski et al., 2024).

When should children start taking these meds?

A recent study investigated the effect of age at treatment onset on increases in brain iron content and its impact on the function of dopamine neurons in patients with ADHD. There were two interesting discoveries: The duration of the treatment did not significantly affect brain iron level but the age of onset of therapy had a major impact on outcome. Children with ADHD who started psychostimulant therapy at 8, or earlier, showed significantly higher iron content in brain regions that have the highest levels of dopamine function, as compared to children with ADHD who started psychostimulant treatment at the age of 9 or later.

Summary

Medication-naïve children with ADHD have lower brain iron content, as compared to normal aged children. ADHD children medicated with standard psychostimulant therapy displayed the same level of brain iron as peers without ADHD. Starting psychostimulant treatment earlier, rather than later, was associated with more brain iron and, according to MRI studies, increased dopamine function. Important caveat: Psychostimulants are not considered a cure for ADHD; it is unknown whether iron levels would decline if the patients discontinued drug therapy.

item.title: More Than a Game: The Therapeutic Benefits of Golf
item.description:
Sport and Competition

More Than a Game: The Therapeutic Benefits of Golf

Golf participation is surging, and providing stress relief.

Posted October 30, 2026

Key points
  • Women, people of color, and young people are taking up golf in record numbers.
  • Golf can promote belonging, stress relief, and mental well-being.
  • Empirical data link golf with confidence, self-worth, and emotion regulation.

Golf is having a cultural moment. Golf used to be a male-only sport associated with exclusive environments, wealth, and serious rules. But the tide is changing. These days, golf is increasingly tied to wellness, diversity, fashion, and fun. Several industry surveys report that young people are taking up golf for stress relief, mental health, social connection, and a chance to unplug outdoors.

Since 2019, women, young people, and people of color have led the growth in golf participation, with each group reaching record or near-record levels. Participation has increased among men as well.

Golf and Well-Being

In a screen-dominated world, golf offers ongoing opportunities to do real things with real people, experience novelty and travel, and be physically active in the outdoors. Golf offers a fun and engaging opportunity to build resilience and personal growth. As an individual, precision sport, it’s you inside your own head. From a mental-game perspective, success rests on the ability to regulate your emotions, stay present in the moment, and be your own best coach – skills that serve us well in golf, life, and at work.

As summarized in Murray and colleagues (2017), empirical data have linked playing golf with enhanced social belonging, intergenerational interaction, confidence, self-worth, interpersonal skills, emotion regulation, and enjoyment.

The positive impact of physical activity on mental-health is well known. Research suggests that if you walk 18 holes, you’ll take between 11,000 and 16,600 steps, and if you take a cart, you’ll get about 6,200. Golf may also help support proprioception, balance, and muscle endurance in older adults (see Murray and colleagues, 2017).

A Sport Psychologist’s Perspective

As a Division 1 golfer turned sport psychologist, I think that the skills built in golf easily translate to life, work, and leadership. You need to change the unhelpful thoughts that pop into your head and tolerate frustration after mistakes. You can’t run it off or rely on a teammate. You practice being present in the moment over each shot. Being your own best coach – as opposed to your own worst critic – helps unlock better scores. You have to get off your phone and get outside for at least an hour and interact with real people — things that many of us crave in a screen-dominated world. In the workplace, golf is still often used for networking, so having some basic golf skills might unlock career opportunities.

Getting Started

Inclusive golf communities are popping up online and in-person, making it easier to find a place to belong in the game. Leagues, teams, regular playing partners, clubs, and off-course golf entertainment venues like simulators provide a place to connect. Foretheladies, No Bunkers No Bogeys, and Youth on Course are just a few examples of inclusive golf communities and initiatives. Golf instructors have taken to YouTube and other online platforms, offering low-fee or free instruction.

If you’re exploring ways to boost your mental well-being, golf might be just what you’ve been looking for.
